buckets.title: Motion in a Plane (CBSE Class XI, Unit II Kinematics) with labelled JEE extensions
buckets.badge_reason: Learners must move between vector algebra and plane kinematics while keeping one frame, one clock and each model's validity conditions in view.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Theory, Unit II Kinematics, Chapter 3 Motion in a Plane

conventions.statement: Declare one x-y frame (origin and axis directions) before writing any component; every component of one problem uses that frame.
i-hat and j-hat are unit vectors along the declared x and y axes.

scope.covers: Scalars and vectors, equality, multiplication by a real number, graphical and analytical addition and subtraction, resolution into rectangular components, motion in a plane with constant acceleration, projectile motion and uniform circular motion, as listed by the CBSE 2026-27 curriculum and the NCERT chapter; five JEE extension microtopics are carried as labelled extensions.

capabilities.action: Classify a physical quantity as scalar or vector, draw a displacement from its end points alone, and judge whether two vectors are equal.
capabilities.success_criterion: Names direction as the deciding property, gives the same displacement for every path between fixed end points, separates path length from displacement magnitude, and calls two vectors equal only when magnitude and direction both match.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Unit II Chapter 3: scalar and vector quantities; position and displacement vectors; equality of vectors

capabilities.action: Predict the magnitude, direction and physical kind of a vector multiplied by a real number, including a negative number, zero, or a multiplier that carries its own dimension.
capabilities.success_criterion: Gives |lambda| times the original magnitude, keeps the direction for a positive multiplier and reverses it for a negative one, returns the null vector for zero, and names the new quantity from the product of dimensions.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Unit II Chapter 3: multiplication of vectors by a real number

capabilities.action: Add and subtract vectors by drawing them head to tail (or as a parallelogram from a common tail) and read the resultant's size and direction from the drawing.
capabilities.success_criterion: Places each tail at the previous head, draws the resultant from the first tail to the last head, forms A - B as A + (-B), and bounds the resultant between the difference and the sum of the magnitudes.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Unit II Chapter 3: addition and subtraction of vectors

capabilities.action: Resolve a plane vector into signed rectangular components from its magnitude and angle, and rebuild the magnitude and angle from the components.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Unit II Chapter 3: unit vector; resolution of a vector in a plane, rectangular components

microtopics.title: Scalars and vectors; position and displacement vectors; equality of vectors
microtopics.badge_reason: Each idea is a single definition, but learners carry over the everyday habit of reading distance travelled as displacement, which the first exercises are built to expose.
entry_assumptions: Can measure a length and state a direction such as east or 30 degrees from a reference line.
Can mark a point on a grid relative to a chosen origin.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Because a vector carries a direction as well as a magnitude, the displacement between two positions is fixed by the end points alone, so it differs from the path length whenever the object changes direction.

teaching_path.action: Sort quantities into scalars, which have magnitude only, and vectors, which have magnitude and direction and add by the triangle (or parallelogram) law.
teaching_path.why_valid: These are the textbook definitions every later vector operation relies on.
teaching_path.output: two labelled lists: magnitude-only quantities and magnitude-plus-direction quantities

teaching_path.action: Fix a reference point as origin so each position of the object can be drawn as an arrow from it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A displacement is read off two positions, so both positions must be located from one agreed point.
teaching_path.output: origin O with the initial position P and final position Q marked

teaching_path.action: Draw the displacement as the single straight arrow from P to Q and check it against several different routes from P to Q.
teaching_path.why_valid: The displacement vector joins the initial and final positions and does not depend on the path actually taken between them.
teaching_path.output: one arrow PQ shared by every route, such as PABCQ, PDQ and PBEFQ

teaching_path.action: Compare each route's path length with the length of arrow PQ.
teaching_path.why_valid: Path length equals the displacement magnitude only if the object never changes direction; in all other cases the path length is greater.
teaching_path.output: path length >= |PQ|, with equality only for the straight route

teaching_path.action: Test two arrows for equality by comparing both magnitude and direction, sliding one parallel to itself onto the other if needed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Two vectors are equal if and only if magnitude and direction match; free vectors may be shifted parallel to themselves, but a vector whose line of application matters may not.
teaching_path.output: equal or not equal, with the failing property named

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Path length and the magnitude of displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A runner completes exactly one lap of a closed track and stops at the start line. What are the path length and the magnitude of the displacement?
misconceptions.repair: Displacement depends only on the end points, which coincide here, so it is zero; the path length is the whole lap. The two agree only when the motion never changes direction.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Two arrows of the same length are equal vectors.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One displacement is 5 m east and another is 5 m north. Are they equal vectors?
misconceptions.repair: No. Equality needs the same magnitude and the same direction; these share only the magnitude.

exit_task.prompt: A student walks 30 m east and then 40 m north. Without calculating, say whether the magnitude of the displacement is less than, equal to or greater than the 70 m walked, and name what fixes the displacement.

answer.summary: Less than 70 m, because the student changed direction; the displacement is fixed only by the start and end points.
reasoning: The path turns through a corner, so the path length exceeds the displacement magnitude.
The displacement is the straight arrow from the start point to the end point, whatever route joins them.
answer.check: A straight walk to the same end point would have a path length equal to the displacement magnitude.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer compares two lengths qualitatively and states no computed value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Anchors the scalar/vector split and the path independence of displacement to verified NCERT text so that the vector-algebra microtopics can build on them.

microtopics.title: Multiplication of vectors by real numbers
microtopics.badge_reason: One rule with three cases; the difficulty is only in not writing a negative magnitude and in tracking the new dimension when the multiplier carries a unit.
entry_assumptions: Can draw a vector as an arrow whose length stands for its magnitude.
Can multiply units, for example (m/s) x s = m.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Multiplying a vector by a real number rescales its magnitude by the number's size and keeps or reverses its direction by the number's sign, so a negative multiplier never makes a negative magnitude.

teaching_path.action: Split the multiplier into a sign and a size.
teaching_path.why_valid: Size and sign change different properties of the arrow, so they are handled separately.

teaching_path.action: Stretch or shrink the arrow by the size of the multiplier.
teaching_path.why_valid: The magnitude of lambda A is |lambda| times the magnitude of A.

teaching_path.action: Keep the arrow's direction for a positive multiplier, reverse it for a negative one, and collapse it to the null vector for zero.
teaching_path.why_valid: A negative multiplier gives the opposite direction; multiplying by zero gives the null vector.
teaching_path.output: lambda > 0: same way; lambda < 0: opposite way; lambda = 0: 0 vector

teaching_path.action: Multiply the dimensions to name the resulting quantity.
teaching_path.why_valid: The dimension of lambda A is the product of the dimensions; a constant velocity times a duration is a displacement.

teaching_path.action: Check against the textbook case A multiplied by 2.
teaching_path.why_valid: 2A is in the same direction as A with twice its magnitude.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Multiplying by a negative number gives a vector with a negative magnitude.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What is the magnitude of -3A if |A| = 2 m?
misconceptions.repair: Magnitudes are never negative: |-3A| = 3 x 2 m = 6 m. The minus sign only turns the vector to point opposite to A.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A scalar multiplier must be a pure number, so a vector times a scalar is always the same kind of quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A velocity of 4 m/s north is multiplied by 5 s. What kind of quantity results?
misconceptions.repair: The multiplier carries a dimension, so the product is a displacement, 20 m north: dimensions multiply.

exit_task.prompt: A velocity of 3 m/s pointing east is multiplied by -2 s. State the magnitude, the direction and the kind of physical quantity of the result.

answer.summary: A displacement of 6 m pointing west.
reasoning: Size: 2 s x 3 m/s = 6 m.
Sign: the multiplier is negative, so the direction reverses from east to west.
Dimension: (m/s) x s = m, a displacement.
answer.check: The magnitude stays positive; only the direction carries the minus sign.

microtopics.research_contribution: Records the sign, size and dimension rules for scalar multiples with the null-vector edge case, each tied to a verified quote.

microtopics.title: Addition and subtraction of vectors: graphical method
microtopics.badge_reason: The construction is mechanical, but learners keep adding magnitudes as numbers and confuse the resultant of two velocities with the velocity of one object relative to another.
entry_assumptions: Can draw an arrow to scale and measure its length and angle.
Can reverse a vector and scale it by a real number.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Placing vectors head to tail makes the resultant the single arrow from the first tail to the last head, so its size depends on the angle between the vectors and lies between the difference and the sum of their magnitudes; subtracting is adding the reversed vector.

teaching_path.action: Choose a starting point and a scale for the drawing.
teaching_path.why_valid: Every arrow must use the same scale so lengths can be compared.
teaching_path.output: origin O and a length scale

teaching_path.action: Draw A, then draw B with its tail at A's head, and join the tail of A to the head of B.
teaching_path.why_valid: This line is the sum R of A and B.
teaching_path.output: R = A + B from tail of A to head of B

teaching_path.action: Redraw A and B from a common tail and complete the parallelogram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The parallelogram diagonal and the triangle construction give the same resultant.

teaching_path.action: Subtract by reversing B and adding.
teaching_path.why_valid: The difference A - B is defined as A + (-B).

teaching_path.action: Check the resultant's length against the sum and the difference of the magnitudes.
teaching_path.why_valid: A side of a triangle is never longer than the sum of the other two nor shorter than their difference; equality holds only for collinear vectors.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The resultant of two velocities acting on one object is the same thing as the velocity of one object relative to another.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Rain falls with velocity v_r and wind adds velocity v_w to the drops. Is the drops' velocity v_r + v_w or v_r - v_w?
misconceptions.repair: Two velocities acting on one object combine as v = v1 + v2; the relative velocity of object 1 with respect to object 2 is the different vector v12 = v1 - v2.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The magnitude of a resultant is the sum (or difference) of the two magnitudes.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A 3-unit and a 4-unit vector are perpendicular. Is their resultant 7 units long?
misconceptions.repair: No. The resultant is a triangle side or parallelogram diagonal, whose length is not a simple sum of side lengths; 7 units arises only when the vectors point the same way.

exit_task.prompt: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at one point. Between what least and greatest values can the magnitude of their resultant lie, and in which arrangement is each reached?

answer.summary: From 1 N (forces opposite) to 7 N (forces in the same direction).
reasoning: The resultant's length lies between the difference and the sum of the magnitudes.
4 N - 3 N = 1 N when the forces are antiparallel.
3 N + 4 N = 7 N when the forces are parallel.
answer.check: Both extremes need collinear forces, which is when equality holds in the triangle inequality.

microtopics.research_contribution: Ties the triangle and parallelogram constructions, commutativity, associativity, subtraction and the triangle inequality to verified NCERT quotes and names the v1 + v2 versus v1 - v2 confusion.

microtopics.title: Resolution of vectors into components
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners reach for A cos(theta) automatically, then lose the sign in other quadrants or treat the number A_x as if it were itself a vector.
entry_assumptions: Can find the sides of a right triangle from its hypotenuse and one angle.
Can add vectors head to tail and scale them by real numbers.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Any plane vector splits into multiples of two non-collinear directions; with the perpendicular unit vectors i and j the multipliers become the signed components A cos(theta) and A sin(theta), which hold the same information as the magnitude and angle.

teaching_path.action: Fix the x-axis and y-axis and the unit vectors i and j along them.
teaching_path.why_valid: A unit vector has magnitude one, no dimension and only specifies a direction.

teaching_path.action: Write A as the sum of a multiple of i and a multiple of j.
teaching_path.why_valid: Any plane vector is a sum of real multiples of two non-zero vectors with different directions.

teaching_path.action: Find the multipliers from the magnitude and the angle with the x-axis.
teaching_path.why_valid: Simple trigonometry on the right triangle gives the components.
teaching_path.output: A_x = A cos(theta), A_y = A sin(theta)

teaching_path.action: Read each component's sign from the quadrant of theta.
teaching_path.why_valid: A component can be positive, negative or zero depending on theta.

teaching_path.action: Rebuild the magnitude and angle from the components.
teaching_path.why_valid: Either description specifies the vector completely.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The component A_x is itself a vector.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Is A_x a vector, or is A_x i the vector?
misconceptions.repair: A_x is a signed number; A_x i is the component vector. Only the product with the unit vector has a direction.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Components are always positive, because they are lengths of triangle sides.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A 200 m displacement points at 315 degrees from the +x axis. What is the sign of its y-component?
misconceptions.repair: Negative: A_y = A sin(315 degrees) < 0. A component's sign depends on theta, and a component can also be zero.

exit_task.prompt: A displacement of 10 m points at 210 degrees measured anticlockwise from the +x axis. Without a calculator, state the sign of each rectangular component and explain how you know.

reasoning: 210 degrees lies between 180 and 270 degrees, the third quadrant.
There cos(theta) and sin(theta) are both negative, so A_x = A cos(theta) < 0 and A_y = A sin(theta) < 0.
answer.check: Drawing the arrow shows it pointing left and down, which agrees with both signs.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: Only the signs of the components are asked for; no component value is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Connects the general two-direction resolution, the unit-vector form and the magnitude-angle form through verified NCERT quotes, with the sign and scalar-component traps each tied to a card.

microtopics.title: Vector addition: analytical method
microtopics.badge_reason: The algebra is routine, but choosing the correct angle for the law of cosines and keeping component signs straight across many vectors trips learners.
entry_assumptions: Can resolve a vector into signed rectangular components and rebuild its magnitude and angle.
Can add vectors head to tail.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Because each component of a resultant is the sum of the corresponding components, vectors are added exactly by adding numbers axis by axis, and for two vectors the same geometry gives R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta) with theta measured tail to tail.

teaching_path.action: Declare one pair of axes for all the vectors.
teaching_path.why_valid: Components can be summed only if they refer to the same axes.
teaching_path.output: x and y axes shared by A, B, C, ...

teaching_path.action: Resolve every vector and add the x-components and the y-components separately.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each component of the resultant is the sum of the corresponding components.

teaching_path.action: Rebuild the resultant's magnitude and angle.
teaching_path.why_valid: The magnitude-angle description follows from the components.

teaching_path.action: For exactly two vectors, use the law of cosines with the tail-to-tail angle.
teaching_path.why_valid: The parallelogram geometry gives R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta).

teaching_path.action: Compare with the textbook boat example: 25 km/h north with a 10 km/h current 60 degrees east of south.
teaching_path.why_valid: The angle between north and 60 degrees east of south, tail to tail, is 120 degrees.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The magnitude of a resultant is the sum or difference of the magnitudes.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Is |A + B| = |A| + |B| for two vectors at 90 degrees?
misconceptions.repair: No. The resultant is a parallelogram diagonal, whose length is not a simple sum of the sides; here R^2 = A^2 + B^2.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The angle in the law of cosines is whatever angle appears between the arrows in the problem's picture.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A boat heads north and the current flows 60 degrees east of south. What theta goes into R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta)?
misconceptions.repair: theta is the angle between the vectors drawn from a common origin: north and 60 degrees east of south are 120 degrees apart, not 60 degrees.

exit_task.prompt: Add A = 3i + 4j and B = -i + 2j by components, and give the magnitude of the resultant.

answer.check: R is shorter than |A| + |B| = 5 + sqrt5 = 7.24, as it must be.

microtopics.research_contribution: Gives the exact component method and the law of cosines verified wording, with the textbook boat example pinning the tail-to-tail angle convention.

microtopics.title: Motion in a plane: position, displacement, velocity and acceleration vectors
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners import two one-dimensional habits: treating average speed as the size of average velocity, and expecting velocity and acceleration to lie on one line.
entry_assumptions: Can find a displacement from two position vectors.
Can differentiate simple polynomials in t.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Velocity and acceleration in a plane are rates of change of vectors, so average velocity uses the displacement, instantaneous velocity is the limit of that ratio and points along the tangent, and acceleration can point at any angle to the velocity.

teaching_path.action: Write the position as r(t) = x(t) i + y(t) j in a fixed frame.
teaching_path.why_valid: Resolution holds at every instant.

teaching_path.action: Form the average velocity over an interval from the displacement.
teaching_path.why_valid: Average velocity is displacement divided by the interval.

teaching_path.action: Let the interval shrink to zero to get the velocity at an instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity; it is tangent to the path.

teaching_path.action: Repeat on the velocity to get the acceleration.
teaching_path.why_valid: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the interval.

teaching_path.action: Check against NCERT Example 3.4: r = 3.0t i + 2.0t^2 j + 5.0 k.
teaching_path.why_valid: Differentiating twice gives the textbook's acceleration.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are the same.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A cyclist rides out and back to the start in 10 min. Are the average speed and the average velocity's magnitude equal?
misconceptions.repair: No. Average speed divides the path length; average velocity divides the displacement, here zero. Average speed is greater than or equal to the average velocity's magnitude, equal only when path length equals displacement magnitude.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Velocity and acceleration always point along the same line, as in one-dimensional motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At the top of a projectile's path, the velocity is horizontal. Must the acceleration be horizontal too?
misconceptions.repair: No. In two or three dimensions velocity and acceleration may make any angle between 0 and 180 degrees; only in one dimension are they collinear.

exit_task.prompt: A particle goes once round a circle of radius R at constant speed, taking time T. State its average velocity and its average speed over that revolution, and explain the difference.

answer.summary: Average velocity is zero; average speed is 2 pi R / T.
reasoning: After one revolution the particle is back where it started, so the displacement and the average velocity are zero.
The path length is the circumference 2 pi R, so the average speed is 2 pi R / T.
They differ because the path length exceeds the displacement whenever the direction changes.
answer.check: Average speed must be at least the magnitude of the average velocity, and 2 pi R / T > 0 agrees.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is zero by the displacement argument and a symbolic expression; no number is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Records the average/instantaneous velocity and acceleration definitions, the tangent direction, and the two carried-over one-dimensional errors, each with a verified quote.

microtopics.title: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners apply the constant-acceleration equations without checking that the acceleration is constant, and lose the link between the axes by not reusing one time.
entry_assumptions: Can use v = u + a t and s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 in one dimension.
Can resolve vectors into x and y components.
microtopics.inferential_jump: When the acceleration vector is constant, plane motion splits into two simultaneous one-dimensional constant-acceleration motions along perpendicular axes, coupled only by the time they share.

teaching_path.action: Confirm the acceleration is constant and fix the axes.
teaching_path.why_valid: The kinematic equations for uniform acceleration hold only then; uniform circular motion is excluded.

teaching_path.action: Write the vector equations and resolve them.
teaching_path.why_valid: The vector equations need no choice of axes and may be resolved along any two independent axes.

teaching_path.action: Solve the axis that carries the given condition for t.
teaching_path.why_valid: The condition on one coordinate fixes the common time.

teaching_path.action: Reuse that t on the other axis.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both components describe the same instant.

teaching_path.action: Recombine the components into a speed or position.
teaching_path.why_valid: A plane state needs both components at one time.
teaching_path.output: speed = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2) at t = 6 s

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The acceleration alone fixes the shape of the trajectory.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two stones fall under the same gravity, one dropped and one thrown sideways. Do they follow the same shape of path?
misconceptions.repair: No. The shape also depends on the initial position and velocity: under the same gravity the path can be a straight line or a parabola.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The constant-acceleration equations work for any motion whose acceleration has constant size.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: May r = r0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t^2 be used for uniform circular motion, where |a| is constant?
misconceptions.repair: No. There the acceleration's direction keeps changing, so the acceleration vector is not constant and the equations do not apply.

exit_task.prompt: A particle starts from rest at the origin with constant acceleration a = (2 i + 1 j) m/s^2. Where is it at t = 2 s?

reasoning: Both use the same t = 2 s.
answer.check: Starting from rest, the particle moves along the direction of a, and (4, 2) is parallel to (2, 1).

microtopics.research_contribution: Anchors the vector constant-acceleration equations, their axis independence and their exclusion of circular motion to verified NCERT text, with Example 3.5 as the shared-time model.

grade9v3:interactive_idea.learner_manipulates: The launch angle and the launch speed, plus a switch that raises or lowers the landing ground relative to the launch point.
grade9v3:interactive_idea.becomes_visible: Equal-time dots along the path with a constant horizontal velocity arrow and a shrinking then reversing vertical arrow; a ghost path for the complementary angle landing at the same point but peaking at a different height; and the level-ground flight-time value drifting away from the true flight time once the landing height differs.

microtopics.title: Projectile motion
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners must hold one model (no air resistance, a_x = 0, a_y = -g) while choosing events on the vertical axis, reusing their time horizontally, and rejecting the level-ground shortcuts whenever the landing height differs.
entry_assumptions: Can solve constant-acceleration motion in a plane with a shared time.
Can resolve a launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Once air resistance is neglected, a projectile is uniform horizontal motion plus vertical motion with constant acceleration g sharing one clock, so every event time comes from the vertical motion and the path is a parabola.

teaching_path.action: State the model: air resistance negligible, +y upward.
teaching_path.why_valid: Then only gravity acts after launch.

teaching_path.action: Resolve the launch velocity and write the velocity components.
teaching_path.why_valid: The x-component remains constant; only the y-component changes, like free fall.
teaching_path.output: v_x = v0 cos(theta0), v_y = v0 sin(theta0) - g t

teaching_path.action: Eliminate t between x(t) and y(t).
teaching_path.why_valid: Both coordinates share one time.
teaching_path.output: y = (tan theta0) x - g x^2/(2 (v0 cos theta0)^2), a parabola

teaching_path.action: Find the event times from the vertical motion.
teaching_path.why_valid: The top has v_y = 0; level-ground landing has y = 0 again.

teaching_path.action: Multiply the constant v_x by the flight time.
teaching_path.why_valid: Horizontal motion is uniform.
teaching_path.output: R = v0^2 sin(2 theta0)/g, largest at 45 degrees

teaching_path.action: Check against NCERT Example 3.8: 28 m/s at 30 degrees.
teaching_path.why_valid: The flight time formula reproduces the textbook value.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Two launches with the same range follow the same path.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ball launched at 15 degrees and one at 75 degrees, same speed, land at the same point. Do they rise equally high?
misconceptions.repair: No. The ranges are equal but the maximum heights differ; the 75 degree path is far higher and takes longer.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The level-ground time-of-flight and range formulas apply whatever the landing height.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A stone is thrown from a cliff and lands below the launch point. May T_f = 2 v0 sin(theta0)/g be used?
misconceptions.repair: No. That formula assumes landing at the launch elevation; for a different landing height solve y(t) = landing height.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: 45 degrees always gives the greatest range.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does 45 degrees still give the maximum range once air resistance is included?
misconceptions.repair: No. The 45 degree result holds only when air resistance is neglected; with it, the best angle is somewhat smaller.

exit_task.prompt: Two balls are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at 30 degrees and one at 60 degrees. Compare their ranges, their maximum heights and their times of flight, with reasons.

answer.summary: Equal ranges; the 60 degree ball rises higher and stays in the air longer.
reasoning: R = v0^2 sin(2 theta0)/g, and sin 60 = sin 120, so the ranges are equal.
The vertical launch component v0 sin(theta0) is larger at 60 degrees, so the top is higher.
T_f = 2 v0 sin(theta0)/g is larger at 60 degrees for the same reason.
answer.check: Complementary angles sharing a range agrees with 45 degrees plus and minus 15 degrees giving equal ranges.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The comparison is qualitative and states no computed value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Ties the projectile model's assumption, component equations, parabola, flight time, range and their level-ground and no-drag limits to verified sources, with an interactive design idea.

relations.expression: |lambda A| = |lambda| |A|; lambda A points along A if lambda > 0 and opposite to A if lambda < 0
relations.meaning: A real multiplier rescales a vector's magnitude by its size and keeps or reverses the direction by its sign; a multiplier with a dimension also changes the kind of physical quantity.

symbols.meaning: real multiplier, possibly carrying a physical dimension

conditions: lambda is a real number; lambda = 0 gives the null vector, whose direction cannot be specified.
The dimension of lambda A is the product of the dimensions of lambda and A.

derivation.action: Write the multiplier as its sign times its size |lambda|.
derivation.why_valid: The size and the sign act on different properties of the vector.

derivation.action: Scale the length of A by |lambda|.
derivation.why_valid: Multiplying by a positive number changes the magnitude by that factor.

derivation.action: Apply the sign to the direction.
derivation.why_valid: A negative multiplier gives the opposite direction with magnitude |lambda| |A|.
derivation.output: lambda < 0 => lambda A antiparallel to A

limits: The rule does not assign a direction to the null vector produced by lambda = 0.
It describes multiplication by a scalar only; it says nothing about products of two vectors.
checks: The result's magnitude is never negative, whatever the sign of lambda.
The unit of the result is the unit of lambda times the unit of A.

relations.expression: R = A + B, drawn with the tail of B at the head of A; A + B = B + A; (A + B) + C = A + (B + C)
relations.meaning: The sum of two vectors is the arrow from the tail of the first to the head of the second when they are placed head to tail; the order and the grouping of the additions do not change the resultant, and the parallelogram construction gives the same result.

symbols.unit_or_domain: vectors of one kind and dimension
same kind and dimension as A and B

conditions: The vectors are free vectors, so each may be moved parallel to itself to place it head to tail.
The vectors added must be of the same kind and dimension; adding any two vectors is not meaningful.

derivation.action: Draw A with its tail at a chosen point O.
derivation.why_valid: A free vector may be drawn from any point.

derivation.action: Move B parallel to itself so its tail sits at the head of A.
derivation.why_valid: Shifting a free vector parallel to itself leaves it unchanged.

derivation.action: Join the tail of A to the head of B.
derivation.why_valid: That line is defined as the sum of A and B.

derivation.action: Repeat with B first.
derivation.why_valid: The same R is obtained, so addition is commutative.

limits: A drawing gives the resultant only to the accuracy of the drawing.
The law does not apply to a localised vector whose line of application matters.
checks: |A| - |B| <= |R| <= |A| + |B| in magnitude.
Reversing the order of addition must reproduce the same R.

relations.meaning: Subtracting a vector means adding its reverse, and adding a vector to its own reverse gives the null vector, which has zero magnitude.

symbols.unit_or_domain: vectors of one kind and dimension

symbols.meaning: vector of the same magnitude as B, pointing the opposite way

conditions: -B has magnitude |B| and the direction opposite to B.
The null vector has zero magnitude, so its direction cannot be specified.

derivation.action: Form -B by reversing B.
derivation.why_valid: Multiplying by -1 reverses a vector without changing its magnitude.

derivation.action: Add A and -B head to tail.
derivation.why_valid: The difference is defined as that sum.

derivation.action: Set B = A.
derivation.why_valid: Equal and opposite vectors give a resultant of zero magnitude.

limits: A - B and B - A are opposite vectors, not equal ones.
checks: (A - B) + B returns A.
|A - B| equals |A + B| only in special orientations, not in general.

relations.meaning: A vector in a plane can be written as the sum of real multiples of any two given vectors of that plane, so two independent directions are enough to describe every vector in it.

symbols.meaning: two given vectors in the plane
real multipliers found by the resolution

conditions: a and b must be non-zero vectors in the same plane with different directions.

derivation.action: Draw A from O and draw lines through O parallel to a and b.
derivation.why_valid: The two directions span the plane when they are not collinear.

derivation.action: Complete the parallelogram with A as its diagonal.
derivation.why_valid: The parallelogram law writes A as the sum of two vectors along the reference lines.

derivation.action: Express each side as a real multiple of a or b.
derivation.why_valid: A vector parallel to a is a real multiple of a.
derivation.output: OP = lambda a, OQ = mu b => A = lambda a + mu b

limits: If a and b are collinear the resolution fails for any A off their line.
checks: Recombining lambda a + mu b head to tail must reproduce A.

relations.expression: A = A_x i + A_y j, with A_x = A cos(theta) and A_y = A sin(theta)
relations.meaning: Along the perpendicular unit vectors i and j, the multipliers are the rectangular components, found by trigonometry from the magnitude A and the angle theta that A makes with the x-axis.

symbols.meaning: angle of A measured from the positive x-axis

symbols.unit_or_domain: real numbers, unit of the quantity

symbols.meaning: unit vectors along x and y

conditions: i and j are unit vectors: magnitude one, no dimension or unit.
A component can be positive, negative or zero depending on theta.

derivation.action: Choose a = i and b = j in the two-direction resolution.
derivation.why_valid: i and j are non-zero and perpendicular, so they satisfy its condition.

derivation.action: Project A onto each axis with the right triangle it forms.
derivation.why_valid: Adjacent side = hypotenuse x cos(theta); opposite side = hypotenuse x sin(theta).
derivation.output: A_x = A cos(theta), A_y = A sin(theta)

limits: The formulas need theta measured from the positive x-axis; an angle measured from another line must be converted first.
checks: The two component formulas together must give back the magnitude A.
theta = 90 degrees gives A_x = 0.

relations.expression: A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2); tan(theta) = A_y / A_x
relations.meaning: The magnitude-and-angle description and the component description carry the same information, so either can be recovered from the other.
conditions: A_x and A_y are components along perpendicular axes; their signs, which depend on theta, fix the quadrant of theta.

derivation.action: Square and add the component formulas.
derivation.why_valid: cos^2 + sin^2 = 1.

derivation.action: Divide the component formulas.
derivation.why_valid: sin/cos = tan.

limits: tan(theta) alone cannot distinguish angles 180 degrees apart; the signs of the components decide.
checks: A is never smaller than |A_x| or |A_y|.

relations.expression: R = A + B => R_x = A_x + B_x, R_y = A_y + B_y
relations.meaning: Each component of a resultant is the sum of the corresponding components of the vectors added, and the method extends to adding and subtracting any number of vectors.

symbols.meaning: signed rectangular components of A and B
symbols.unit_or_domain: real numbers, unit of the quantity
real numbers, unit of the quantity

conditions: All components are taken along the same pair of axes.
Components carry their signs, which depend on each vector's angle with the x-axis.

derivation.action: Write both vectors in unit-vector form on one set of axes.
derivation.why_valid: Resolution gives A = A_x i + A_y j and B = B_x i + B_y j.
derivation.output: A = A_x i + A_y j, B = B_x i + B_y j

derivation.action: Add and group the i terms and the j terms.
derivation.why_valid: Vector addition is commutative and associative, so terms may be regrouped.

limits: The component sums give R exactly; the accuracy of the graphical method is limited by the drawing.
checks: Subtraction uses the same rule with B's components negated.
R_x = 0 means R lies along the y-axis.

relations.expression: R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta); R/sin(theta) = A/sin(beta) = B/sin(alpha)
relations.meaning: For two vectors at angle theta, the law of cosines gives the magnitude of their resultant and the law of sines gives its direction.

symbols.meaning: angle between A and B drawn from a common origin
angles the resultant makes with A and with B

conditions: theta is the angle between A and B when both are drawn from a common origin (tails together).

derivation.action: Draw A and B from a common origin O at angle theta and complete the parallelogram.
derivation.why_valid: The diagonal OS is the resultant by the parallelogram law.

derivation.action: Resolve along A: the diagonal has components A + B cos(theta) and B sin(theta).
derivation.why_valid: B's projection on A's line is B cos(theta); the perpendicular part is B sin(theta).

derivation.action: Expand and use cos^2 + sin^2 = 1.
derivation.why_valid: Algebra.

limits: For more than two vectors the component method is the practical route.
checks: theta = 0 gives R = A + B; theta = 180 degrees gives R = |A - B|.
theta = 90 degrees gives R^2 = A^2 + B^2.

relations.meaning: Average velocity over an interval is the displacement divided by the length of that interval.
conditions: delta r is the displacement between the two positions, which depends only on the end points and not on the path.

derivation.action: Take positions r at time t and r' at t'.
derivation.why_valid: Displacement is the change in position.
derivation.output: delta r = r' - r, delta t = t' - t

derivation.action: Divide the displacement by the interval.
derivation.why_valid: Average velocity is defined as displacement per unit time.

limits: Average velocity says nothing about the motion inside the interval.
checks: A closed route gives v_avg = 0 whatever the path length.

relations.expression: v = lim(delta t -> 0) delta r / delta t = dr/dt; v_x = dx/dt, v_y = dy/dt
relations.meaning: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the interval shrinks to zero; its direction at any point is along the tangent to the path, in the direction of motion.

symbols.meaning: position vector as a function of time

conditions: The limit is taken at the instant of interest, as the time interval approaches zero.

derivation.action: Shrink the interval around the instant.
derivation.why_valid: The average velocity approaches a limiting value.

derivation.action: Apply the limit to each component of r.
derivation.why_valid: r = x i + y j with fixed unit vectors.

limits: Requires the position to be known as a function of time near the instant.
checks: The velocity arrow drawn at a point of the path is tangent to the path there.

relations.expression: a_avg = delta v / delta t; a = dv/dt
relations.meaning: Average acceleration in the plane is the change in velocity divided by the interval; the change can be in magnitude, direction or both.
conditions: In two or three dimensions the velocity and acceleration may make any angle from 0 to 180 degrees.

derivation.action: Subtract the velocity vectors at the two instants.
derivation.why_valid: Vector subtraction is addition of the reverse.

derivation.action: Divide by the interval.
derivation.why_valid: Average acceleration is defined as velocity change per unit time.

limits: A constant speed does not imply zero acceleration, because delta v includes a change of direction.
checks: Units: m/s divided by s gives m/s^2.

relations.expression: v = v0 + a t; v_x = v_0x + a_x t, v_y = v_0y + a_y t
relations.meaning: When the acceleration is constant, the average acceleration over any interval equals it, so the velocity changes linearly with time, component by component.
conditions: The acceleration vector is constant in magnitude and direction over the interval.
The vector equation needs no choice of axes and may be resolved along any two independent axes.

derivation.action: Take a constant acceleration a.
derivation.why_valid: Over any interval the average acceleration then equals a.

derivation.action: Write the average acceleration from t = 0 to t.
derivation.output: a = (v - v0)/t => v = v0 + a t

limits: Not valid for uniform circular motion, where the acceleration has constant magnitude but changing direction.
checks: a = 0 gives constant velocity.
Each component obeys the one-dimensional form.

relations.meaning: With constant acceleration the displacement is the average velocity (v0 + v)/2 times the interval, so motion in a plane is two separate simultaneous one-dimensional constant-acceleration motions along perpendicular directions.

symbols.meaning: elapsed time shared by both components

conditions: The acceleration is constant over the interval; for arbitrary motion only the definitions of average velocity and average acceleration hold.
Both component equations use the same elapsed time t.

derivation.action: Use the average velocity for linearly changing velocity.
derivation.why_valid: With constant a, the average of v over the interval is (v0 + v)/2.

derivation.action: Substitute v = v0 + a t.
derivation.why_valid: The velocity at time t is known from the first relation.

derivation.action: Resolve along x and y.
derivation.why_valid: The vector equation may be resolved along any two independent axes.

limits: The trajectory's shape is not fixed by a alone; it also depends on r0 and v0.
checks: Setting a = 0 gives straight-line motion at constant velocity.
Time found from one axis must be reused on the other.

relations.expression: a_x = 0, a_y = -g; v_x = v0 cos(theta0), v_y = v0 sin(theta0) - g t
relations.meaning: A projectile's motion is two simultaneous independent components: horizontal with no acceleration, so v_x stays constant, and vertical with the constant acceleration of gravity, like free fall.
conditions: Air resistance is assumed to have a negligible effect on the projectile's motion.

derivation.action: Take +x horizontal and +y upward; after release only gravity acts.
derivation.why_valid: Air resistance is neglected in this model.

derivation.action: Apply v = v0 + a t to each component.
derivation.why_valid: Constant acceleration on each axis.
derivation.output: v_x = v0 cos(theta0), v_y = v0 sin(theta0) - g t

limits: Does not hold when drag or propulsion acts during flight.
checks: v_x is the same at every point of the flight.
v_y = 0 at the top of the path.

relations.expression: y = (tan theta0) x - g x^2 / (2 (v0 cos theta0)^2)
relations.meaning: Eliminating time between the two component positions gives the equation of a parabola, so the path of a projectile in this model is a parabola.

symbols.meaning: horizontal and vertical position from the launch point

conditions: Air resistance is neglected, so a_x = 0 and a_y = -g throughout the flight.

derivation.action: Write both positions.
derivation.why_valid: Constant-acceleration equations on each axis.
derivation.output: x = v0 cos(theta0) t, y = v0 sin(theta0) t - (1/2) g t^2

derivation.action: Eliminate t using t = x / (v0 cos theta0).
derivation.why_valid: Both coordinates share one time.
derivation.output: y = (tan theta0) x - g x^2 / (2 (v0 cos theta0)^2)

limits: With air resistance the path is not this parabola.
checks: y = 0 at x = 0 and at x = R.
The coefficient of x^2 is negative, so the path opens downward.

relations.expression: t_m = v0 sin(theta0)/g, T_f = 2 t_m = 2 v0 sin(theta0)/g; R = v0^2 sin(2 theta0)/g, R_m = v0^2/g at theta0 = 45 degrees
relations.meaning: On level ground the time of flight is twice the time to the top, by the symmetry of the parabola, and the range for a given launch speed is largest at 45 degrees; angles 45 degrees plus and minus alpha give equal ranges.

symbols.meaning: maximum range for the given v0

conditions: The projectile lands at the same elevation as it was launched; otherwise the time-of-flight formula does not apply.
Air resistance is neglected; with air resistance the angle of maximum range is somewhat smaller than 45 degrees.

derivation.action: Set v_y = 0 for the top.
derivation.why_valid: The vertical velocity vanishes at maximum height.

derivation.action: Set y = 0 again for the landing time.
derivation.why_valid: Same launch and landing level.

derivation.action: Multiply the constant v_x by T_f.
derivation.why_valid: Horizontal motion is uniform.
derivation.output: R = v0 cos(theta0) x 2 v0 sin(theta0)/g = v0^2 sin(2 theta0)/g

limits: Not for landings above or below the launch level.
checks: sin(2 theta0) is largest, 1, at 45 degrees.
sin(2(45 + alpha)) = sin(2(45 - alpha)), so complementary angles share a range.

questions.stem: Establish the following vector inequalities geometrically or otherwise : (a) |a+b| <= |a| + |b| (b) |a+b| >= ||a| - |b|| (c) |a-b| <= |a| + |b| (d) |a-b| >= ||a| - |b||. When does the equality sign above apply?
conditions: a and b are any two vectors of the same kind.

answer.summary: Draw a, b and a + b (or a - b = a + (-b)) as a triangle; the triangle's side rules give all four inequalities, and equality holds only when a and b are collinear.
reasoning: Place a and b head to tail; the resultant a + b is the third side, so |a + b| <= |a| + |b|.
The same triangle gives |a + b| >= ||a| - |b||, since one side is never shorter than the difference of the other two.
Replace b by -b, which has the same magnitude, to obtain (c) and (d) for a - b.
The triangle collapses to a line only when a and b are parallel or antiparallel, which is when the equality signs apply.
answer.check: Setting b parallel to a turns (a) into an equality and (d) into an equality simultaneously.

reasoning_route.action: Draw a, b and a + b as the three sides of one triangle.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Head-to-tail addition makes the resultant the closing side.

reasoning_route.action: Apply the triangle side rules to that triangle, then to the triangle for a + (-b).
reasoning_route.why_valid: -b has the same length as b, so the same rules bound |a - b|.

reasoning_route.action: Identify when the triangle degenerates.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A triangle becomes a straight line only when the sides are collinear.
reasoning_route.output: equality for collinear a and b

questions.stem: i and j are unit vectors along x- and y- axis respectively. What is the magnitude and direction of the vectors i + j, and i - j ? What are the components of a vector A = 2i + 3j along the directions of i + j and i - j ? [You may use graphical method]
conditions: i and j are perpendicular unit vectors along the x- and y-axes.

answer.summary: |i + j| = sqrt2 at 45 degrees with the x-axis; |i - j| = sqrt2 at -45 degrees with the x-axis. The components of A along i + j and i - j are 5/sqrt2 and -1/sqrt2.
reasoning: i + j has components (1, 1): magnitude sqrt(1 + 1) = sqrt2, tan(theta) = 1, theta = 45 degrees.
i - j has components (1, -1): magnitude sqrt2, theta = -45 degrees.
Write A = lambda(i + j) + mu(i - j): lambda + mu = 2 and lambda - mu = 3, so lambda = 5/2 and mu = -1/2.
Along i + j the component is lambda |i + j| = (5/2) sqrt2 = 5/sqrt2; along i - j it is mu |i - j| = -1/sqrt2.
answer.check: (5/sqrt2)^2 + (-1/sqrt2)^2 = 13 = 2^2 + 3^2, so the new components rebuild |A|.

questions.stem: For two vectors A and B, |A + B| = |A - B| is always true when
options: (c) |A| = |B| != 0 and A and B are parallel or anti parallel
(d) when either A or B is zero.
conditions: theta is the angle between A and B drawn from a common origin.

reasoning: |A + B|^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta).
A - B = A + (-B), and -B makes angle 180 - theta with A, so |A - B|^2 = A^2 + B^2 - 2AB cos(theta).
The two are equal exactly when AB cos(theta) = 0: theta = 90 degrees, or A = 0, or B = 0.
Equal magnitudes alone, (a) or (c), do not make cos(theta) zero.
answer.check: For parallel equal vectors |A + B| = 2A while |A - B| = 0, so (c) fails.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Reversing B changes cos(theta) to -cos(theta).
